name: Mënsch (Luxembourgish Trick-Taking)
description: MÃ«nsch is a traditional trick-taking game from Luxembourg, belonging to the Ombre/Solo family of European card games. Played by four players with a 32-card deck, it features the 'Mensch' (the Queen of Clubs) as the permanent highest trump card, regardless of the declared suit. It is a game of shifting alliances where a bidder can choose to play alone (Solo) or call a partner to help them win a majority of tricks.

history.origins: Derived from the ancient Spanish game 'Hombre' (L'Homme), which spread through Europe and evolved into regional variants like German Solo and Luxembourgish MÃ«nsch.
timeline: 1700s: Ombre-derived games become popular in the Low Countries.
1800s: MÃ«nsch stabilizes in Luxembourg with the Queen of Clubs as the fixed top trump.
1950s: Club competitions in Luxembourg formalize the contract bidding hierarchy.
Present: Remains a core part of Luxembourgish national identity in card clubs.
history.cultural: Played in local cafÃ©s across Luxembourg, often using specific tokens called 'Marques'.
history.evolution: The name 'MÃ«nsch' (meaning Human/Person) refers to the highest trump card, emphasizing the game's human-centric bidding hierarchy.

setup.deck: 32 cards. Remove 2-6 from a standard deck.
setup.dealing: Each player receives 8 cards (dealt in batches of 4).

rules.objective: Win the number of tricks specified in your contract (usually 5+).
rules.gameplay: Standard trick-taking rules: Must follow suit (remember Qâ™£ is a trump, not a club). Highest trump wins.
keyRules: 32-card deck: remove 2s through 6s; Queen of Clubs (Mensch) is always the highest trump.
Second-highest trump is the 7 of the trump suit; then A, K, Q, J, 10, 9, 8. Non-trump suits rank A, K, Q, J, 10, 9, 8, 7.
Deal 8 cards each in batches of 4, clockwise from left of dealer.

Bidding: Half/After (5 tricks with partner, clubs trump); Five/Six/Seven/Solo (alone, bidder chooses trump); Five After/Six After/Seven After (alone, clubs trump). Order: Half < After < Five < Five After < Six < Six After < Seven < Seven After < Solo.
Must follow suit if possible; Queen of Clubs counts as trump. Highest trump wins trick; if no trump, highest card of led suit wins. Winner of trick leads next.

strategy.basic: If you hold the Mensch (Qâ™£), you have the ultimate weapon. Save it to kill a trick where you suspect an opponent is playing their highest trump. If you are a secret partner, don't reveal yourself until the card you were called with is played; use your trumps to help the leader win early tricks.
strategy.intermediate: Contract Selection: Only bid 'Solo' if you have at least 4 trumps (including high ones) and at least one Ace in a side suit. If you have a weak hand but hold the Mensch, bid 'Half' and call an Ace you don't have to secure a strong partner.
strategy.advanced: The 'Forced Club' lead: Since the Mensch is always a trump, leading a small Club can force the opponents to reveal if they are holding the Mensch early. If they win with it, you know they are out of their most powerful card for the end-game.
tips: In MÃ«nsch, 7s of the trump suit are often second-highest trumpsâ€”don't underestimate them!
If playing Solo, your goal is to 'exhaust' the combined trumps of the three opponents. Keep leading trumps until they are gone.

variations.name: No-bid pays two chips
variations.description: Some play that if no one bids, the holder of the Queen of Clubs names trumps and calls a partner; if the calling team takes four tricks or fewer, the caller and partner each pay two chips (same as Half/After) instead of one.
variations.emptyOverridesReason: Variant only changes chip payment rule; no engine overrides needed.
